chief_complaint: pleuritic chest pain, low-grade fever, and pericardial friction rub 3 weeks after heart bypass surgery
hpi_details: 63F post-CABG 3 weeks ago presenting with autoimmune pericarditis, elevated inflammatory markers, and moderate pericardial effusion responsive to high-dose Aspirin and Colchicine.
ideas: She thinks one of her new bypass grafts has already clogged up or that she is suffering another heart attack.
concerns: She is terrified of having to go back into the operating room and have her breastbone cracked open a second time.
expectations: She hopes to have an ultrasound of her heart today and get stronger pain pills to relieve the sharp catching pain when she breathes.

available_results.value: Moderate circumferential pericardial effusion measuring 14 mm, without chamber collapse or tamponade physiology

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Postpericardiotomy Syndrome (Dressler-type) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management is high-dose NSAIDs (e.g., aspirin) plus colchicine for several weeks, with close monitoring for progression to tamponade via serial exam and echocardiography.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: pleuritic chest pain, low-grade fever, and pericardial friction rub 3 weeks after heart bypass surgery
Key HPI features: 63F post-CABG 3 weeks ago presenting with autoimmune pericarditis, elevated inflammatory markers, and moderate pericardial effusion responsive to high-dose Aspirin and Colchicine.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Postpericardiotomy Syndrome Dressler.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Postpericardiotomy Syndrome (Dressler-type).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Postoperative infection (mediastinitis) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Signs of tamponade (hypotension, muffled heart sounds) — the pericardial effusion can occasionally become large enough to compress the heart.
management_principles: Treat with high-dose aspirin/NSAIDs plus colchicine; obtain echocardiogram to assess effusion size and rule out tamponade
Refer to cardiology if effusion is large, symptoms fail to improve, or tamponade physiology develops
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune inflammatory reaction to cardiac surgery, occurring weeks afterward, causing pleuritic chest pain, low-grade fever, and a pericardial friction rub — usually responsive to NSAIDs and colchicine.
red_flags: Signs of tamponade (hypotension, muffled heart sounds) — the pericardial effusion can occasionally become large enough to compress the heart

must_ask.say: How many weeks ago was your bypass surgery?
Does the pain improve when you sit up and lean forward?
Have you had a low-grade fever?
Does the pain get worse with deep breaths?
Has your surgical incision been healing normally?

history.answer: Ever since three days ago, I have had a sharp chest pain that gets noticeably worse whenever I take a deep breath.
It started gradually about three days ago while I was sitting on the sofa reading a book.
It is mostly right in the middle of my chest and slightly over to the left side, behind my breastbone.
It feels like a sharp, stabbing ache rather than a heavy pressure or tearing sensation.
No, it stays right in the center of my chest and does not shoot to my left arm, jaw, or back.
The pain is pretty much constant throughout the day, but it spikes whenever I breathe deeply or cough.
It is about a 4 out of 10 when I sit still, but it jumps to a 7 out of 10 if I try to take a big breath.
Walking around makes it ache a bit more because I breathe harder, but resting does not make it go away completely.
It hurts much worse when I lie flat on my back, and leaning forward brings noticeable relief; pressing on my ribs does not change the pain.
No, eating does not trigger it, and I have no heartburn, sour taste, or pain with swallowing.
I feel slightly short of breath because it hurts to take a deep breath, but I have had no cold sweats, nausea, or dizziness.
I have had a mild, low-grade fever and felt warm for the past couple of days, but I have no cough or phlegm.
No, I have not had a runny nose, sore throat, or any stomach flu since my surgery.
I had open-heart bypass surgery three weeks ago, but neither of my legs is swollen, red, or painful.
No, I checked my skin and there are no rashes, red spots, or blisters anywhere on my chest.
I feel anxious because of my recent heart surgery, but I have not had panic attacks, tingling in my fingers, or a sudden sense of doom.
I do not have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, and I have never smoked.
Before my bypass surgery I had angina that felt like a dull, heavy pressure when walking uphill, which felt completely different from this sharp pain.

history.answer: No, I have not hit my chest, lifted anything heavy, or strained my upper body since coming home.
The surgical incision on my chest looks clean and dry, with no spreading redness or fluid oozing out.
I was convinced one of the bypass veins must have blocked up or that I'm having another heart attack so soon after surgery.
I'm terrified that something went wrong with the surgery and they'll have to cut my chest open all over again.
I was hoping you could do an ultrasound to make sure my new bypass is intact and give me stronger painkillers so it doesn't hurt every time I breathe.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses like hypertension, diabetes, or lung disease.
Aside from the coronary artery bypass graft surgery three weeks ago, I have never had any other surgeries.
I was discharged with only occasional acetaminophen as needed, and I am not taking any other prescription or herbal medicines.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I do not drink alcohol.
I am a retired teacher living at home with my supportive husband.
There is no family history of early heart disease, blood clots, or sudden unexplained deaths.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/76 mmHg in both arms, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 37.8°C.
Comfortable at rest leaning slightly forward, alert, with no diaphoresis, pallor, or acute distress.
Jugular venous pulse is normal at 2 cm above the sternal angle with no jugular venous distension.
Well-healing median sternotomy incision without erythema, warmth, or drainage; chest wall palpation does not reproduce the chest pain.
High-pitched, scratchy, triphasic friction rub heard best along the left lower sternal border with the patient leaning forward, with normal heart sounds and no murmurs.
Resonant to percussion symmetrically throughout all lung fields.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with good air movement and no crackles, wheezes, or pleural rubs.
Soft, non-tender throughout with no epigastric tenderness, organomegaly, or guarding.
No pitting edema in either lower extremity.
Calves are soft, symmetric, and non-tender bilaterally with negative Homans sign.
No rashes, blisters, or skin lesions across the chest wall or trunk.
